w:r.w:t: The Impact of Telemedicine on the Treatment of Covid-19:
A Retrospective Study in Collapsed Brazilian Cities
Claudia Solmucci, MD; ; Gelse Campos, MD; Guilherme Succi, MD; Irene Cunha, MD; Priscila Rabelo, MD; Diego Albs & Cols.

The acute respiratory syndrome caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus was declared a pandemic in March 2020 [1-3], severely impacting global public health and economy. In January 2021, the healthcare system in the city of Manaus, (Amazonas, Brazil) collapsed. Hospitals became overcrowded, with no available beds and a shortage of oxygen for critically ill patients, many of whom had to be transferred out of the city or succumbed without access to treatment. Doctors from various specialties and other healthcare professionals organized for humanitarian aid and formed a task force for remote care. Doctor8, a medical software initially developed as a cloud-based medical record system, was made available and adapted for telemedicine services. Over 11 months of service, a vast amount of data was stored on this digital platform, enabling the analysis and review of results and enriching the discussion on treatment with repurposed drugs. Approximately 12,000 families were served, benefiting an estimated 36,000 people. The mortality rate (0.36%) observed in a group of 2,220 patients positively supports the impact of telemedicine and favors early pharmacological treatment with repurposed drugs, including Ivermectin, Hydroxychloroquine, and Nitazoxanide.

In March 2020, the World Health Organization alerted us to the pandemic of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, causing the Coronavirus Disease Syndrome (COVID-19) [1-3], severely affecting public health and the global economy. Initially, healthcare professionals were caught off-guard by this new nosological entity with unknown pathogenesis, diagnosis, and treatment. In January 2021, the healthcare system in the city of Manaus, (Amazonas, Brazil) collapsed. Hospitals were overcrowded, with no available beds and a lack of oxygen for critically ill patients, many of whom had to be transferred to other cities or perished without access to treatment. Doctors from various specialties and other healthcare professionals organized themselves for humanitarian aid and formed a task force for remote care.

The solution to this deadlock was to address the long-standing demand by the medical community for the use of Telemedicine, which has been regulated by the Federal Council of Medicine (CFM) since 2002, under Resolution No. 1.643. The text defines this technology as "the practice of Medicine through the use of interactive communication methodologies, audiovisual, and data, aimed at health assistance, education, and research."

The Federal Government authorized its provisional/emergency use through Law No. 13,989, dated April 15, 2020, as an alternative to in-person patient care during the pandemic. Additionally, the Ministry of Health published Ordinance No. 467 on March 20, 2020, dealing with the matter. The Federal Council of Medicine (CFM), in turn, issued Official Letter CFM No. 1756 on March 19, 2020, recognizing the practice and regulating the ethical aspects related to procedures conducted virtually.

It is estimated that during the pandemic, over 7.5 million Telemedicine consultations were carried out in Brazil by more than 52,200 doctors. Of these, 87% were for initial consultations [4]. The data from the Brazilian Association of Telemedicine and Digital Health Companies show that the resolution rate of these consultations was 91%, meaning most patients had their complaints resolved and did not need to seek in-person emergency care as a second step. The association estimates that 75,000 lives were saved in Brazil thanks to this technology.

While definitive regulation advances in the National Congress through Bill 1998/2020, one thing is certain: the possibility of providing extended health follow-up through virtual means has proven effective and opened new perspectives for healthcare professionals and patients alike.

Doctor8, a medical software originally developed as a cloud-based medical record system, was made available and adapted for telemedicine services. Over 11 months of service, an enormous amount of data was stored on this digital platform, enabling analysis and review of results, and enriching the discussion on treatment with repurposed drugs. Approximately 12,000 families were served, benefiting an estimated 36,000 people.

The medical campaign involved around 122 medical professionals from various specialties who acted as general practitioners, supported by the Federal Council of Medicine, which ensures medical autonomy in Brazil. This allowed patients access to off-label drug treatment with repurposed antivirals, including Hydroxychloroquine, Ivermectin, Nitazoxanide (with or without Azithromycin), as well as anti-androgens or other drugs with potential cyto-immunoprotective, anti-inflammatory, and/or antithrombotic effects, such as Dexamethasone, Prednisolone, Enoxaparin, Rivaroxaban, vitamin D, bromhexine, colchicine, budesonide, N-acetylcysteine, among others prescribed at clinical discretion.

All patients who received off-label drug treatment were informed and gave their digital consent via the Informed Consent Forms (ICF) [Appendix 1 and 2], attached to the medical questionnaire, as recommended by the Federal Council of Medicine (opinion 04/2020), the Declaration of Helsinki (1964), and the Nuremberg Code (1947).

The recognition by Brazilian society of the work done in Manaus led the medical group to extend their services to other cities severely affected by the pandemic, providing necessary technological and human support to the non-profit non-governmental organization "Médicos Pela Vida," which has been active nationwide since the beginning of the pandemic.

In various cities, the community service also receives support from professional associations and local businesses, such as in Uberaba, Ribeirão Preto, Chapecó, and Itaúna. The platform is also available for use by the SUS in Uberaba in partnership with the municipal government. Professionals from various health sectors assist families, including psychologists, physiotherapists, and nutritionists. A team of non-medical volunteers helps with registration and appointment scheduling, as well as in raising funds for the procurement and distribution of medication and food to underprivileged patients.

Approximately 12,000 families from nearly all Brazilian states were served by the Doctor8 telemedicine platform. It is expected that the campaign has benefited around 36,000 citizens so far, considering the average size of Brazilian families according to 2018 IBGE data [5]. With the emergence of new variants and the start of mass vaccination, the initial questionnaire has been modified to expand understanding of the disease's evolution in all its phases, as well as ongoing prophylaxis and immunization.
Demonstrate the importance of Telemedicine in emergency medical care for sick individuals in areas where doctors are not physically present;
Report the experience of the group of volunteer doctors providing this service;
Evaluate the characteristics of the patients and their clinical evolution;
Measure the mortality rate due to Covid-19 among patient groups according to the start date of treatment;
Analyze the feasibility of remote consultations during a pandemic.

The system uses Node.js as its backend language, with PostgreSQL as the database. Active since 2014, initially used in private practices solely as an electronic medical record, it became a tool for telemedicine following Law No. 13,989, dated April 15, 2020, and the LGPD - General Data Protection Law No. 13,709, dated August 14, 2018 [6-13].

122 doctors from various regions of the country, with validated CRM by the CFM, participated in the study. They signed their documents using digital certificates accredited by ICP Brasil. At the end of the service period and due to professional confidentiality, we sent questions to the doctors regarding patient evolution, treatment type and start, use of antivirals, and occurrence of deaths among patients.
Members of local communities, nursing professionals, physiotherapists, and psychologists guide patients, creating a bridge between volunteer doctors and their patients.

Data was collected retrospectively from January 25, 2021, to December 20, 2021, encrypted, and stored in the cloud. Patients responded to a preliminary clinical questionnaire serving as a digital anamnesis, where, in addition to personal data and symptoms, they declare having been informed and agreeing to off-label treatment and data sharing, meeting legal requirements. The questionnaire is shared and stored in each doctor's Doctor8 system. All healthcare professionals are registered in the system, each having their own virtual clinic where their autonomy is ensured. Consultation data is encrypted and can only be accessed via a personal password, ensuring medical confidentiality. Medical care and collected data are the direct responsibility of the professional. Repurposed drug treatment is offered to all patients seen. The involved doctors are volunteers and share similar, though not identical, clinical guidelines due to patient heterogeneity, socioeconomic conditions, affected cities, etc. Documents and prescriptions, digitally signed on the platform, can be shared with patients, pharmacies, clinics, and laboratories, eliminating the need for travel and speeding up care. The table below illustrates the questionnaire that precedes consultations, enabling statistical analysis after cross-referencing with data provided by doctors post-consultation. The triage through the questionnaire with alert symptoms helps prioritize more severe patients, reducing wait times in these cases and providing timely access to pharmacological treatment.

The data from this type of service are auditable, can be reviewed, and contribute to resolving doubts about treatment with repurposed drugs and other issues still needing resolution in this new disease like Covid-19, which is so polarized where conflicts of interest and even fraud obscure the true outcomes.
Figure 1 - Table with items from the questionnaire used to gather patient information. Symptoms are highlighted in orange to prioritize the care of severe cases.

Out of the total number of volunteer doctors, 66 responded to the questionnaire, from which we extracted data for analysis on 2,220 patients with a confirmed Covid-19 diagnosis via RT-PCR. Of these, 2,212 (99.64%) used one or more antivirals, including Hydroxychloroquine (with or without Azithromycin), and/or Ivermectin, and/or Nitazoxanide. Only 5 (0.22%) did not use antivirals, and 3 (0.13%) discontinued treatment. There were 8 deaths, all involving patients with comorbidities, giving this group a mortality rate of 0.36%. The observed comorbidities included: obesity in 5 patients (71.43%), diabetes in 2 (28.57%), hypertension in 2 (28.57%), and pulmonary emphysema in 1 (12.5%); some with overlapping conditions.

Of the total patients who used antivirals (n=2,212), 415 patients (18.69%) were seen and started treatment within 3 days of symptom onset (D3); 946 patients (42.61%) between 4 and 6 days (D4-D6), and 844 (38.02%) more than 6 days after symptom onset (D6+). Among the patients treated within 3 days of symptom onset, there were no deaths (0%). For the deceased patients, 1 (12.50%) was seen after 4 days of symptom onset, 2 (25.00%) after 5 days, and 5 patients (62.50%) after 7 days.

The average age of patients treated within three days of symptom onset was 40 years (range: 1 to 95 years). In this group, even with 37.35% having comorbidities, no deaths were recorded. Patients treated between four and six days had an average age of 41 years (range: 0 to 88 years), with 41.75% having comorbidities, and 0.32% (3) of them died. Patients treated after more than six days had an average age of 42 years (range: 1 to 84 years), 43.48% had comorbidities, and there were 5 deaths (0.59%). Two of the deceased patients were under 40 years old, obese, and were seen after five days of symptoms. Six of the deceased patients had an average age of 62 years (range: 54 to 73 years) and were seen after more than seven days of symptoms, except for one who was seen after four days.

Figure 2 - Histogram of the number of patients treated (n = 2208), distributed by age. The dashed line represents the average age of the patients (41.68). Fourteen patients did not provide their age and were not included.

Of the patients who died, seven were male and one was female. We treated 122 children and adolescents up to 17 years old, making up 5.5% of the sample, with 1.17% having comorbidities, and no deaths occurred in this group.
In the statistical analysis to assess sample representation with a 95% Confidence Level, we obtained a value of 0.021, which is approximately ~2.1224% for n=2220.
When comparing the groups regarding the occurrence of death and the start of treatment within D0-D3, D4-D6, and >D6, using the Chi-Square Test, we got p≃0.096.

The Doctor8 Telemedicine platform was the digital tool made available to volunteer doctors in Brazil when healthcare services collapsed in Brazilian cities. Despite the heterogeneity due to the urgency of medical attention, it was possible to gather interesting real-time data regarding treatment with repurposed drugs. To expedite consultations and document data, every patient seen through the Doctor8 platform responds to a standard questionnaire previously designed by doctors, covering relevant clinical aspects, specific symptoms, personal history, previous medication use, and patient-related comorbidities.

The Covid-19 pandemic, declared in March 2020, shook the world and impacted the global economy. The lack of knowledge about the disease's mechanisms and the severity of cases leading quickly to death alarmed both doctors and government officials. The frantic search for medications capable of inhibiting viral replication spurred scientists worldwide, and the possibility of using repurposed drugs was soon considered.

Older drugs like Hydroxychloroquine, with an established safety profile in other infectious diseases like malaria [14] and more recently, Zika virus infection [15], emerged as a promise after the publication of observational studies by professors Didier Raoult [16-17] and Vladimir Zelenko in the USA [18], who used Hydroxychloroquine combined with Azithromycin and achieved a significant reduction in mortality rates. The publication of work by Leon Caly (Australia) proving in vitro inhibition of viral replication [19] encouraged its off-label use, and hundreds of studies have been published on the subject since then.

The Doctor8 Telemedicine platform accumulated a vast amount of data over 11 months of service, stored in the cloud and accessible for research purposes. The cross-referencing of data provided by doctors after consultations is computed electronically, allowing for dynamic, real-time analysis. The possibility of correcting potential biases stemming from the complexity of the topic makes the analysis of results transparent and objective.

The data collected indicates that treatment with repurposed drugs reduced mortality by 7.5 times compared to the official data from the Ministry of Health for the same period (2.8%) [20]. Of the 8 patients who died, 6 of them (75%) were seen after 6 days of symptom onset. No patient treated within 3 days of symptom onset died.

Obesity and male gender were factors associated with death in young adult patients. Obesity was the most frequently associated comorbidity with death [21-22]. The mortality rate was 7 times higher in males than in females. These findings are consistent with the literature, but regarding gender, the male predominance was 5.3 times higher than reported by Takehiro Takahashi et al. [23-24].

The comparison between the time from symptom onset to medical consultation highlights the importance of early treatment in relation to mortality rates. These results corroborate literature data showing that pharmacological treatment with repurposed drugs with potential antiviral effects should be initiated within the first 72 hours of symptoms [25-49].
The data underscores the significance of beginning pharmacological treatment within 72 hours of symptom onset, as no deaths occurred among those treated within this window.

The Doctor8 telemedicine platform ensured legal security, compliance with current laws, and facilitated quick medication prescriptions, clinical monitoring, and the sharing of digitally signed documents, tests, and prescriptions.
Telemedicine effectively bridges the geographical gap between doctors and patients, providing comprehensive and prompt care during pandemics.
The platform also serves as an innovative tool for encouraging prospective research by gathering uniform and controlled data in both emergency and non-emergency contexts.

A cloroquina e a hidroxicloroquina são medicamentos disponíveis há muitos anos para a prevenção e tratamento da malária e algumas doenças reumáticas, como artrite reumatóide e lúpus. Apesar de serem bem tolerados, eles podem causar efeitos colaterais como: redução dos glóbulos brancos, disfunção do fígado, disfunção cardíaca e arritmias, e alterações visuais por danos à retina.Apesar de não haver, até o momento, estudos suficientes para garantir certeza de melhora clínica dos pacientes com COVID-19, quando tratados com cloroquina ou hidroxicloroquina, há diversos estudos em andamento ao redor do mundo. Cientistas chineses demonstraram a capacidade dessas drogas de inibir a replicação do coronavírus em laboratório (in vitro) e um estudo francês mostrou que a eliminação do coronavírus da garganta de portadores da COVID-19 se deu de forma mais rápida com a utilização da combinação de hidroxicloroquina e o antibiótico azitromicina, quando comparados a pacientes que não usaram as drogas.

Termo de consentimento livre e esclarecido para o uso não estabelecido em bula, de drogas (off label) na vigência de infecção suspeita ou confirmada pelo Covid-19 (SARS COV 2) conforme critério médico.
